question: How do layerwise initialization scalings partition infinite-width three-layer ReLU networks into lazy, critical, and strongly feature-learning training regimes?

key_findings.claim: ReLU homogeneity reduces common three-layer initialization and output scalings to two independent phase coordinates, gamma-2 and gamma-3, after time normalization.
key_findings.evidence: The normalized gradient flow absorbs the original alpha and beta scales into kappa parameters; assuming equal hidden widths and beta-2 proportional to beta-3 leaves two power-law exponents that distinguish trajectories up to time rescaling.

key_findings.claim: Each hidden layer empirically has linear, critical, and condensed regimes defined by its relative weight displacement as width grows.
key_findings.evidence: The slope S_Wi of log relative displacement versus log width is negative, zero, or positive when displacement tends to zero, remains order one, or diverges. Width sweeps from 100 to 10,000 estimate separate boundaries for W1 and W2.

key_findings.claim: Different layers of the same network can occupy different regimes.
key_findings.evidence: Because the empirical W1 and W2 zero-slope boundaries differ in the gamma-2/gamma-3 plane, the phase diagram contains mixed regions where one layer is effectively linear while the other undergoes order-one or diverging feature movement.

key_findings.claim: The phase partition approximately transfers from a four-point one-dimensional regression problem to MNIST.
key_findings.evidence: Full-batch MSE experiments on both datasets sweep the same widths and coordinates; the MNIST zero-crossing patterns qualitatively resemble the synthetic map.

key_findings.claim: Strongly nonlinear regions exhibit condensation into a small number of weight orientations.
key_findings.evidence: First-layer weight-and-bias vectors visually cluster along isolated directions, while a cosine-similarity statistic for large second-layer input vectors increases in corresponding phase regions across eight initialization repeats.

key_findings.claim: The boundaries are empirical extrapolations, not an established infinite-width phase theorem.
key_findings.evidence: Finite widths up to 10,000 are fit with log-log slopes; stars use linear interpolation and dashed boundaries are explicitly described as conjectural. Statistical uncertainty is sparsely reported and the MNIST comparison is qualitative.

key_findings.claim: The diagram diagnoses parameter motion rather than downstream generalization.
key_findings.evidence: The conclusion proposes studying how regimes affect generalization as future work; no test accuracy or controlled comparison establishes that condensation or a mixed regime is beneficial.

method.core_idea: Normalize a three-layer ReLU gradient flow by width-dependent initialization exponents, then empirically infer layerwise phase boundaries from parameter displacement.
method.mechanism: Positive homogeneity isolates two exponent coordinates. For every coordinate, full-batch training is repeated over increasing equal layer widths; the log-log slope of final relative weight change assigns each layer to lazy, critical, or condensed behavior. Angular plots and cosine similarity diagnose condensation.
assumptions: Both hidden layers have equal width and the outer initialization scales obey beta-2 equals a width-independent constant times beta-3.
Continuous-time gradient-flow scaling is represented by finite-step full-batch gradient descent.
Power-law slopes over widths 100 to 10,000 reliably extrapolate to infinite width.
ReLU homogeneity and Gaussian initialization are essential to the two-coordinate normalization.

techniques.role: Collapses multiple initialization and output scales into independent width exponents.
Classifies linear, critical, and condensed dynamics for each hidden layer.
Estimates asymptotic boundaries by sweeping coordinates and widths.
Detects clustering of active weights through scatter plots and cosine similarity.

evaluations.setting: Three-layer fully connected ReLU regression on four one-dimensional points, widths 100-10,000.
evaluations.metric: Layerwise relative-displacement exponent, learned interpolation, and weight orientations.
evaluations.result: The scan separates lazy, critical, and divergent movement and reveals smooth-to-spline-like function changes plus condensation.
evaluations.baseline: Known NTK, He, LeCun, Xavier, and mean-field scaling points located in the same coordinates.

evaluations.setting: Three-layer ReLU classification on MNIST with full-batch MSE.
evaluations.metric: Estimated log-log displacement slopes and interpolated zero boundaries for both layers.
evaluations.result: The qualitative phase topology resembles the four-point result and includes mixed layerwise regimes.

evaluations.setting: Second-layer condensation on the four-point task at width 10,000.
evaluations.metric: Mean absolute pairwise cosine among the half of input-weight rows with largest norm.
evaluations.result: Eight-run averages show high angular alignment in the predicted condensed region.
evaluations.baseline: Linear-region coordinates with near-orthogonal random orientations.

limitations: The main claim is empirical despite referring to the infinite-width limit.
Only equal-width, three-layer, fully connected ReLU networks and constrained initialization families are covered.
Full-batch MSE on four points and MNIST is far from practical stochastic training.
Boundary uncertainty, convergence diagnostics, seed variability, and optimizer discretization sensitivity are not comprehensively quantified.
Condensation is not causally tied to simplicity or generalization.
The phase coordinates rely on positive homogeneity and do not directly apply to sigmoid, tanh, attention, or normalized residual architectures.
failure_modes: Finite-width crossover can look like a power law over the measured range but change asymptotically.
Training different scalings to unequal optimization accuracy can contaminate displacement estimates.
Learning-rate discretization can create apparent nonlinear movement absent from gradient flow.
Angular alignment can increase because inactive units are filtered or because one direction dominates magnitude.
Unequal layer widths or layerwise optimizers add independent scales not represented by the diagram.
reusable_insights: Classify feature learning layer by layer; one label for a deep network can hide mixed dynamics.
Normalize parameterizations before comparing initialization regimes so differences are not mere time rescalings.
Report finite-width slope stability and confidence intervals before naming an asymptotic phase.
Pair parameter displacement with functional and generalization metrics.
Map standard parameterizations into a shared exponent space to make theory comparisons explicit.
open_questions: Can the conjectured boundaries be proved for three-layer gradient flow?
How do unequal widths, SGD, normalization, residual connections, and adaptive optimizers change the map?
Which mixed layerwise regimes improve sample efficiency or generalization?
Is orientation condensation a cause or consequence of learned low-complexity functions?
Can comparable phase coordinates be derived for transformers?

competitive_landscape.title: Phase Diagram for Two-layer ReLU Neural Networks at Infinite-width Limit
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct precursor defining linear, critical, and condensed regimes for one hidden layer.
competitive_landscape.difference: Luo et al. establish the two-layer map with stronger analysis; Zhou et al. add a second hidden layer and discover mixed layerwise regimes but rely mainly on empirical boundaries.

competitive_landscape.title: Tensor Programs IV: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: General competing parameterization theory for feature learning at infinite width.
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang and Hu characterize stable versus feature-learning limits for arbitrary-depth architectures and identify maximal-update parameterization; this paper produces a fine-grained empirical phase map for equal-width three-layer ReLU networks.

competitive_landscape.title: Three Mechanisms of Feature Learning in an Analytically Solvable Model
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later phase-diagram work identifying mechanistically distinct kinds of feature learning.
competitive_landscape.difference: That work derives alignment, disalignment, and rescaling mechanisms in a solvable model; Zhou et al. classify layer movement and condensation numerically without resolving multiple mechanisms inside the nonlinear region.

competitive_landscape.title: Global Convergence and Rich Feature Learning in L-Layer Infinite-Width Neural Networks under mu Parametrization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current theory joining deep infinite-width feature learning with global convergence.
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. prove convergence and rich feature learning for arbitrary depth under mu-parameterization; the 2022 paper supplies an empirical taxonomy across a wider initialization plane but no comparable guarantee.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The work claims the first empirical infinite-width phase diagram for three-layer ReLU networks, showing independent layer regimes and condensation.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The layerwise mixed-regime observation and normalization map are useful exploratory tools. Calling the result an infinite-width phase diagram is stronger than the evidence: boundaries are extrapolated from a modest finite-width grid, and current mu-parameterization theory offers deeper guarantees. Its value is hypothesis generation rather than settled asymptotics.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete 12-page extraction, including normalization, all phase scans, condensation measures, MNIST replication, conclusion, and references. The primary two-layer precursor, Tensor Programs IV, later solvable-mechanism work, and 2025 deep mu-parameterization theory were checked on official arXiv, PMLR, and OpenReview records on 2026-08-23.
